title: 1962 Seattle decision whether to allocate scarce chronic dialysis using social-worth criteria

decision_cutoff.date_or_period: 1962, during the early operation of the Seattle Artificial Kidney Center
decision_cutoff.definition: The decision how to choose among medically eligible people with end-stage kidney failure when chronic haemodialysis can sustain life but available machines, staff and funding can treat only a small fraction of candidates.

packets.masking_note: Names Seattle, chronic haemodialysis and the Admissions and Policy Committee.
Names, city and treatment removed; retains the structure of a scarce life-sustaining treatment, medical eligibility and proposed lay social-worth selection.

expected_constitutional_constraints: Real scarcity means not every eligible person can be treated immediately; the Code must not evade the allocation problem by demanding an unavailable option.

Medical criteria relevant to ability to benefit may justify different treatment priority, but income, occupation, education, social prestige or perceived community usefulness require an independent moral justification and cannot silently become proxies for human worth.

Dependants and third-party consequences are morally relevant harms but must not automatically make a parent, breadwinner or socially connected person intrinsically more valuable than a childless or low-status person.
Where medically eligible candidates are materially similar, a fair random/queue process may be less arbitrary than opaque comparative judgements of social worth.
Allocation criteria, conflicts, evidence and appeal/review mechanisms should be explicit because life-or-death scarcity power cannot mark its own examination paper.
Scarcity itself creates a positive institutional duty to expand capacity where reasonably feasible rather than treating rationing rules as a permanent substitute for supply.

sources.citation: Shana Alexander, 'They Decide Who Lives, Who Dies', Life magazine, 9 November 1962
sources.use_note: Contemporaneous account of the Seattle Admissions and Policy Committee and the social information considered when selecting among medically screened candidates. The article's framing and observations are contemporary journalism, not a neutral administrative transcript.

sources.citation: University of Washington historical materials on Belding Scribner, chronic haemodialysis and the Seattle Artificial Kidney Center
sources.use_note: Documents the development of the Scribner shunt/chronic dialysis programme and severe early capacity constraints.

sources.citation: Albert R. Jonsen, historical scholarship on the Seattle dialysis selection committee and the emergence of bioethics
sources.use_note: Used to distinguish the real resource scarcity from later criticism of lay social-worth ranking.
